newsitem.title: USA: House denies extra time for Gingrich probe.
newsitem.headline: House denies extra time for Gingrich probe.

text.p: The House voted Tuesday to deny extra time for the ethics committee to wind up its work on the investigation of Newt Gingrich.

The virtual party line vote of 223-205 to reject a proposal by a bipartisan ethics subcommittee investigating charges against Gingrich came less than three hours after Gingrich was re-elected speaker for the new Congress.
The committee last month set final action on the Gingrich case -- a House vote on punishment -- no later than Jan. 21.

On Tuesday special counsel James Cole, with the backing of the four members of the subcommittee, said to ensure a fair and orderly process "it will be necessary for the vote on the House floor to occur after Jan. 21, 1997."
To accommodate the request Democrats called for a change in proposed House rules that would have put the current ethics committee out of business at the end of Jan. 21.
It was this change that the House rejected. The two Republicans on the investigating subcommittee, Reps. Porter Goss of Florida and Steven Schiff of New Mexico, both voted for the extra time.

Representative Ben Cardin, the senior Democrat on the bipartisan subcommittee, called the Jan. 21 date "unrealistic" and said it did not give enough time to prepare for public hearings on the sanctions against Gingrich for which additional witnesses might need to be called.

Representative Jim McDemott of Washington, top Democrat on the full committee, said Gingrich's attorney called Cole Monday to say he would not be ready for hearings until Jan. 13 and needed time to prepare.

"We are being forced into a schedule which is being designed for political damage control," he said, charging that Republicans wanted to have the House vote on Jan. 20 -- presidential inauguration day.
But ethics committee member David Hobson, R-Ohio, complained that the Democratic motion, which contained no end-date, meant the affair could "go on forever and ever."
Republican Leader Dick Armey told reporters later, "Cole, the counsel, does not schedule the floor of the House of Representatives."
In his statement Cole denied that any member of the subcommittee had tried to improperly delay work on the Gingrich investigation.

In the runup to Gingrich's re-election as speaker Republicans repeatedly said the charges against him were politically motivated and that Democrats wanted to drag out the affair to weaken the speaker.

Gingrich's re-election came as the ethics committee prepared for a procedural meeting in closed session Wednesday to receive the findings of the investigating subcommittee and vote on accepting Gingrich's waiver of a "trial" on the charges, which he admitted Dec. 21.

Gingrich acknowledged he failed to get legal advice to ensure compliance with a ban on use of tax-exempt funds for partisan political activity and gave false information to investigators, which he said was unintentional.
Speculation was the committee would recommend the full House issue a reprimand -- a penalty that would not require Gingrich to step down as speaker.
